question: Q17
answer:
# Answers — 29 CFR § 1910.147 (The Control of Hazardous Energy), July 1, 2014 edition

## 1. Minimum unlocking strength of tagout-device attachment means

**50 pounds** (minimum unlocking strength of **no less than 50 pounds**).

Governing text — § 1910.147(c)(5)(ii)(C) (Substantial):

> "Tagout devices, including their means of attachment, shall be substantial enough to prevent inadvertent or accidental removal. Tagout device attachment means shall be of a non-reusable type, attachable by hand, self-locking, and non-releasable with a minimum unlocking strength of no less than 50 pounds and having the general design and basic characteristics of being at least equivalent to a one-piece, all-environment-tolerant nylon cable tie."

Reading notes that matter for compliance:
- The 50-pound figure is a **floor, not a target**: "no less than 50 pounds." Any attachment means used to secure a tag must not release below that force.
- It attaches to the **attachment means** (the tie/strap/lanyard that fastens the tag), not to the tag's printed face, and it applies to **all** tagout device attachment means. § 1910.147 does not establish separate one-time-use and reusable figures; the phrase "non-reusable type" in the same sentence is a construction requirement on the attachment means, not a second strength value. There is therefore a single strength answer under this section.
- The 50-pound strength requirement sits alongside, not instead of, the other (c)(5)(ii) device criteria: durable (A), standardized by color/shape/format and print-and-tag-construction (B), substantial (C), and identifiable as to the employee applying it (D). § 1910.147(c)(5)(ii) also requires lockout/tagout devices to be singularly identified, to be the only devices used for energy control, and not to be used for other purposes.

## 2. Frequency of employer inspection of the energy-control procedure

**At least annually** — i.e., no longer than 12 months between periodic inspections of each energy control procedure.

Governing text — § 1910.147(c)(6) (Periodic inspection), § 1910.147(c)(6)(i):

> "The employer shall conduct a periodic inspection of the energy control procedure at least annually to ensure that the procedure and the requirements of this standard are being followed."

The interval is only half of the requirement; the qualifiers in (c)(6)(i)(A)–(D) and (c)(6)(ii) are what an inspector will actually check:
- **(c)(6)(i)(A)** The inspection must be performed by an **authorized employee other than the one(s) using** the procedure being inspected (no self-inspection).
- **(c)(6)(i)(B)** The inspection must be conducted **to correct any deviations or inadequacies** identified.
- **(c)(6)(i)(C)** Where **lockout** is used, the inspection must include a review, between the inspector and **each authorized employee**, of that employee's responsibilities under the procedure.
- **(c)(6)(i)(D)** Where **tagout** is used, the inspection must include a review, between the inspector and **each authorized and affected employee**, of that employee's responsibilities, with respect to the elements of the tagout system.
- **(c)(6)(ii)** The employer must **certify** that periodic inspections were performed; the certification must identify the **machine or equipment** on which the procedure was being utilized, the **date** of the inspection, the **employees included**, and the **person performing** the inspection.

Boundary conditions and common errors:
- "At least annually" is a maximum interval, not a fixed calendar date; a 13-month gap is a violation even if the inspection was performed "last year."
- The annual interval applies **per energy control procedure**. § 1910.147(c)(4)(ii) relieves the employer of *documenting* a procedure in the limited single-source/single-equipment case, but it does not create an exemption from the (c)(6) periodic inspection.
- The change-driven obligation in § 1910.147(c)(7)(iii) (retraining when job assignments, machines/equipment/processes, or the energy control procedures change) is a **training** trigger, not an inspection interval. The only stated inspection interval in § 1910.147 is "at least annually."

## 3. Edition / verification statement

The two provisions above are the July 1, 2014 edition text of 29 CFR part 1910 and are unchanged in the current eCFR and in the GovInfo annual editions reviewed (2019 and 2024): § 1910.147(c)(5)(ii)(C) still reads "minimum unlocking strength of no less than 50 pounds," and § 1910.147(c)(6)(i) still reads "at least annually." No amendment has altered either figure, so a program built to the 2014 edition remains aligned with the current federal text on these two points.

## 4. Scope and applicability caveats

- These are the **federal OSHA general-industry** requirements. Roughly half the states and territories operate OSHA-approved State Plans; State Plans must be at least as effective as the federal standard but may adopt different *procedural* requirements (e.g., state-specific inspection documentation forms). The substantive 50-pound and annual figures above are the federal baseline to which any state-plan comparison should be made.
- The Maritime (29 CFR 1915/1917/1918) and Construction (29 CFR 1926) lockout/tagout rules and the electrical standards (29 CFR 1910.269, 1910.333) contain their own device and control requirements; they are outside the scope of this question, which is limited to § 1910.147.
- This answer addresses the two asked figures and their immediate qualifiers only. It is not a full compliance audit of an energy-control program (written procedures, training, hardware inventory, group lockout, contractor coordination, and shift-change provisions under § 1910.147(c)(4), (c)(7), (f), and (g) are separate obligations).

## 5. Answer as stated (for direct use)

| Item | Value | Citation |
|---|---|---|
| Minimum unlocking strength, tagout-device attachment means | **50 pounds** (no less than) | § 1910.147(c)(5)(ii)(C) |
| Employer inspection of the energy-control procedure | **At least annually** (≤ 12 months) | § 1910.147(c)(6)(i) |

question: Q17
answer:
ANSWERS

1. Minimum unlocking strength for tagout-device attachment means: 50 pounds. The regulation sets it as a floor — the attachment means must be "non-releasable with a minimum unlocking strength of no less than 50 pounds." Citation: 29 CFR § 1910.147(c)(5)(ii)(C)(2).

2. Frequency of the employer's periodic inspection of the energy control procedure: at least annually (a recurrence interval not exceeding 12 months). Citation: 29 CFR § 1910.147(c)(6)(i).

REGULATORY TEXT (29 CFR § 1910.147, as printed in the July 1, 2014 annual edition of 29 CFR Parts 1900–1910)

§ 1910.147(c)(5)(ii)(C) Substantial —
"(1) Lockout devices. Lockout devices shall be substantial enough to prevent removal without the use of excessive force or unusual techniques, such as with the use of bolt cutters or other metal cutting tools.
(2) Tagout devices. Tagout devices, including their means of attachment, shall be substantial enough to prevent inadvertent or accidental removal. Tagout device attachment means shall be of a non-reusable type, attachable by hand, self-locking, and non-releasable with a minimum unlocking strength of no less than 50 pounds and having the general design and basic characteristics of being at least equivalent to a one-piece, all-environment-tolerant nylon cable tie."

§ 1910.147(c)(6) Periodic inspection —
"(i) The employer shall conduct a periodic inspection of the energy control procedure at least annually to ensure that the procedure and the requirements of this standard are being followed.
(ii) The periodic inspection shall be performed by an authorized employee other than the ones using the energy control procedure being inspected.
(iii) The periodic inspection shall be designed to correct any deviations or inadequacies identified.
(iv) Where lockout is used for the energy control procedure, the periodic inspection shall include a review between the inspector and each authorized employee, of that employee's responsibilities under the energy control procedure.
(v) Where tagout is used for the energy control procedure, the periodic inspection shall include a review between the inspector and each authorized and affected employee, of that employee's responsibilities under the energy control procedure."

INTERPRETIVE NOTES (needed to read the two numbers correctly)

- 50 pounds is a minimum, not a target or a maximum. An attachment means that releases at less than 50 lbf does not meet (c)(5)(ii)(C)(2); one that releases at 50 lbf or more does, provided it is also non-reusable, hand-attachable, self-locking, non-releasable, and of a design at least equivalent to a one-piece, all-environment-tolerant nylon cable tie. The 50-pound figure applies only to the tagout attachment means; the lockout-device provision in (c)(5)(ii)(C)(1) carries no pound value.
- "At least annually" fixes the maximum interval at 12 months; a shorter interval is compliant, a longer one is not. Paragraphs (c)(6)(ii)–(v) govern who performs the inspection and what it must cover (inspector must be an authorized employee other than the user of the procedure being inspected; review with each authorized employee where lockout is used, and with each authorized and affected employee where tagout is used). They do not alter the interval.

VERIFICATION BASIS

The periodic-inspection sentence above was matched verbatim against a fetched copy of 29 CFR 1910.147 during research (DOE-hosted PDF, sha256 436a6cab3c51). The 50-pound sentence is quoted from the standard's text, which has been unchanged since the 1989 lockout/tagout rulemaking and is identical in the July 1, 2014 annual edition and in current editions; the subsection citation is given so the figure can be confirmed against the printed 2014 volume in a single lookup. No interpretive letters, compliance directives, or later amendments were relied on.

question: Q17
answer:
ANSWERS — 29 CFR § 1910.147, July 1, 2014 edition

| # | Ask | Answer | Cite |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Minimum unlocking strength for tagout-device attachment means | 50 pounds ("no less than 50 pounds") | § 1910.147(c)(5)(i) |
| 2 | Frequency of employer's periodic inspection of the energy control procedure | At least annually (interval between inspections must not exceed 12 months) | § 1910.147(c)(6)(i) |

1. MINIMUM UNLOCKING STRENGTH — 50 POUNDS

Verbatim text, § 1910.147(c)(5)(i): "Tagout devices, including their means of attachment, shall be substantial enough to prevent inadvertent or accidental removal. Tagout device attachment means shall be of a non-reusable type, attachable by hand, self-locking, and non-releasable with a minimum unlocking strength of no less than 50 pounds and having the general design and basic characteristics of being at least equivalent to a one-piece, all-environment-tolerant nylon cable tie."

How to read the figure:
- 50 lb is a FLOOR. The attachment means must resist at least 50 pounds of unlocking force before releasing. There is no upper limit in the standard; a device that resists 80 lb satisfies it.
- The strength requirement is not free-standing. The same sentence requires the attachment means to be non-reusable, attachable by hand, self-locking, and non-releasable. A 50-lb-resistant device that is reusable or requires a tool to attach does not comply.
- "Tagout device attachment means" is the element that secures the tag to the energy-isolating device (e.g., the nylon cable tie of the type the sentence benchmarks against) — not the tag itself.

Citation note (important for verification): the governing paragraph is (c)(5)(i). Some secondary summaries mislabel it as (c)(5)(ii)(C)(2); § 1910.147(c)(5)(ii) is the requirement that the tag identify the employee applying it, and (c)(5)(iii) is the warning-legend requirement. The quoted sentence above is the (c)(5)(i) text.

Do not confuse this with lockout devices: § 1910.147(c)(4)(ii)(C) sets no pound figure for lockout devices, requiring only that they be "substantial enough to prevent removal without the use of excessive force or unusual techniques, such as with the use of bolt cutters or other metal cutting tools." The 50-pound number is specific to tagout attachment means.

2. PERIODIC INSPECTION FREQUENCY — AT LEAST ANNUALLY

Verbatim text, § 1910.147(c)(6)(i): "The employer shall conduct a periodic inspection of the energy control procedure at least annually to ensure that the procedure and the requirements of this standard are being followed."

How to read the interval:
- "At least annually" sets the maximum permissible interval: the gap between successive periodic inspections of a given energy control procedure must not exceed 12 months. Inspecting more often is permitted; inspecting less often is a violation.
- It is not a calendar-year requirement. A rolling 12-month cycle measured from the last inspection satisfies the text.
- The inspection is of the energy control PROCEDURE (its adequacy and whether it and the standard's requirements are being followed), not merely a walk-by of the equipment.

Accompanying requirements in the same paragraph (they do not change the frequency, but a compliant program needs them): § 1910.147(c)(6)(ii) the inspector must be an authorized employee other than the one(s) using the procedure being inspected; (c)(6)(iii) the inspection must correct any deviations or inadequacies found; (c)(6)(iv) where lockout is used, review each authorized employee's responsibilities with that employee; (c)(6)(v) where tagout is used, review each affected employee's responsibilities with that employee; (c)(6)(vi) the employer must certify the inspection, identifying the machine or equipment, the date, the employees included, and the person performing it.

EDITION BASIS (July 1, 2014)

Both paragraphs quoted above originate in the lockout/tagout final rule (54 FR 36644, Sept. 1, 1989) and have not been amended since. The July 1, 2014 annual CFR edition therefore carries the same text and the same two values: 50 pounds and at least annually. The current eCFR text retrieved during research matches, which is consistent with — though not by itself proof of — the 2014 text.

Independent confirmation for a reviewer: eCFR point-in-time view at https://www.ecfr.gov/on/2014-07-01/title-29/section-1910.147 , or the printed volume 29 CFR Part 1910, revised as of July 1, 2014, Subpart J. If a point-in-time check showed different wording, that text would control over this answer; nothing in the record indicates any such difference.

SCOPE BOUNDARIES

- This answers the federal OSHA standard only. OSHA-approved State Plan states must be at least as effective as the federal standard but may word these provisions differently or add requirements; state-plan text is not addressed here.
- Ask 2 is answered for the § 1910.147(c)(6) periodic inspection only. Inspection/inspection-interval duties in other standards (e.g., § 1910.333, § 1910.269, § 1910.217) are not folded into this answer.
- These are the regulatory figures as written; this is not legal advice and does not address letters of interpretation or guidance, which are not the regulation.

question: Q17
answer:
Under 29 CFR § 1910.147, July 1, 2014 edition, the answers are:

1. Minimum unlocking strength for tagout-device attachment means: 50 pounds.
   Pinpoint citation: 29 CFR § 1910.147(c)(5)(i).
   Regulatory text: "Tagout device attachment means shall be of a non-reusable type, attachable by hand, self-locking, and non-releasable with a minimum unlocking strength of no less than 50 pounds and having the general design and basic characteristics of being at least equivalent to a one-piece, all-environment-tolerant nylon cable tie."
   The regulation uses pounds as the unit. The figure is a floor: "no less than 50 pounds." The requirement applies to the means of attachment for a tagout device, not to a separate strength rating for the tag itself.

2. Frequency of the employer's periodic inspection of the energy-control procedure: at least annually.
   Pinpoint citation: 29 CFR § 1910.147(c)(6)(i).
   Regulatory text: "The employer shall conduct a periodic inspection of the energy control procedure at least annually to ensure that the procedure and the requirements of this standard are being followed."
   "At least annually" means the inspection must occur not less than once per 12-month period; it is a maximum interval, not a suggestion. Related requirements in the same paragraph include that the periodic inspection be performed by an authorized employee other than the one using the procedure being inspected, § 1910.147(c)(6)(ii), and that the employer certify the periodic inspections, § 1910.147(c)(6)(iii).

3. Combined answer in the requested format: 50 pounds; at least annually.

For a written procedure or audit checklist, the operative line is: "Tagout device attachment means must be non-releasable with a minimum unlocking strength of no less than 50 pounds; the employer must conduct a periodic inspection of the energy-control procedure at least annually."
